newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Mahathir's coalition seen sweeping Sarawak polls.
newsitem.headline: Mahathir's coalition seen sweeping Sarawak polls.

text.p: Malaysia's timber and oil rich state of Sarawak goes to the polls this weekend for state assembly elections and the main question is whether the ruling coalition will win every seat or lose a couple.
Sarawak Chief Minister Abdul Taib Mahmud's National Front coalition got off to a roaring start by winning 19 seats uncontested last month when candidates filed nomination papers.
"It's going to be really tough," said Lim Guan Eng, deputy leader of the Democratic Action Party (DAP) which is fielding just six candidates. "To be frank, we hope to get one or two (seats)."

Taib, who has headed the Sarawak government since 1981, commanded all 56 seats in the outgoing assembly, spread among four parties in his coalition. Another six seats have been added since the last election in 1991 for a total of 62 seats.
His coalition is allied to Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's federal National Front. The polls are on Saturday and Sunday.
The Borneo based state of Sarawak -- about as large as peninsular Malaysia itself -- is one of the poorest and most undeveloped in Malaysia, despite being rich in resources.

Many of its population of 1.7 million live in longhouses in dense rainforests in the interior. Malaysia is the world's largest exporter of tropical timber and Sarawak accounts for nearly 80 percent of it.
Lim accused Taib of announcing funding projects and spreading campaign funds around to help voters forget they are far less developed than their compatriots on the peninsular.
"It is not only their extensive use of money, but the use of government machinery by the ruling party and the control of the media in Sarawak," he told Reuters in an interview on Friday.
"As we enter the 21st century, Sarawak voters must decide if they want an elective dictatorship or a meaningful democracy," he said.
Sarawak is made up of a dozen or so tribes, with the biggest represented in the coalition by their own parties.
But ever since English adventurer James Brooke, the "white Rajah" of Borneo, conquered the territory in the mid-19th century, colonial resentments have lingered among Sarawakians.
Nowadays, those feelings are sometimes directed at their more prosperous countrymen across the South China Sea in Peninsular Malaysia, political analysts say.
The federal government takes 95 percent of the revenues from oil and gas produced in Sarawak and the opposition says it does not give back an equal amount in development funds.
Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim accused the DAP and independent candidates of resorting to racial issues and slandering the government in the campaign.

"It's easy to gain influence by whipping up racial sentiment and slandering others but it will only be for a while and at the cost of national unity and ultimate destruction," Anwar told a campaign rally in the state on Thursday.
Sarawak did not need an opposition because the parties in Taib's coalition "provide constructive criticism over any issue", the national news agency Bernama quoted him as saying.

The giant Bakun hydroelectric dam -- a $5.5 billion project that will flood an area the size of Singapore and generate 1,800 megawatts of electricity to be sold mostly to Peninsular Malaysia -- has not been much of a campaign issue.
Lim acknowledged that Bakun has been controversial only in Belaga district where it is located. Taib has declared it "a non-issue".
